subject: Accounting
title: Identifying Transactions
description: A micro-lesson that makes Identifying Transactions usable.

hook.text: A business does hundreds of things daily. The accounting cycle asks: which ones count?

buildup.text: Only events that can be measured in money enter the accounting system.

discovery.text: A sale, a purchase, a loan payment—these are transactions. A staff meeting is not.

twist.text: Missing even one transaction can cascade into errors across every financial statement.

climax.text: Source documents like invoices and receipts prove that a transaction actually happened.

punchline.text: No document, no entry. That's the rule.

details.summary: Identifying transactions is the first step of the accounting cycle—determining which economic events qualify as recordable transactions. Not all business activities are transactions; only those that can be measured in monetary terms and affect the accounting equation.
details.whyItMatters: If the wrong events are recorded or the right events are missed, everything built on that data—financial statements, tax returns, management reports—will be wrong from the start.
takeaways: A recordable transaction must be measurable in monetary terms and affect the accounting equation
Source documents like invoices, receipts, and contracts provide evidence that a transaction occurred
Hiring an employee or signing a contract may not be immediate transactions until money or obligations change hands

faq.question: What makes a business event a recordable accounting transaction?
faq.answer: A recordable transaction must involve a measurable exchange of value that changes the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity). Selling goods, paying rent, and borrowing money are transactions. Conversations with customers, signing employment letters, or receiving inquiries are not.

faq.question: What are source documents and why are they important?
faq.answer: Source documents are the original records proving a transaction occurred—invoices, receipts, bank statements, contracts, and purchase orders. They provide the evidence trail that auditors follow and are the basis for accurate journal entries.
